summary: Analyzes actions by or against a Certification Authority or repository manager in the RPKI that could harm the internet number resources of an INR holder. It takes the perspective of the affected holder and is not meant to be comprehensive.

plainLanguage.summary: The RPKI is a set of signed certificates that say which network is allowed to originate a given block of addresses. This document asks what happens when the party holding the signing key does something the address holder did not want, from quietly withholding an object to publishing a forged one. It lists the six things that can be done and traces what each does.

questions: what are adverse actions in rpki
subtitle: What can go wrong in the RPKI when a certificate authority or repository operator acts against the wishes of the address holder.

tldr.problem: The Resource Public Key Infrastructure lets a certificate authority publish, change or withdraw the statements that bind address space to an origin AS. If that authority acts against the wishes of the resource holder, the effect on routing is not well documented.
tldr.mechanism: The document names six adverse actions, from deleting an object to injecting a new one, and works through what each of them does to every kind of object in the repository.
tldr.outcome: The result is a threat model for the RPKI, expressed from the point of view of the affected resource holder, laid out over four organisational scenarios, intended as a basis for designing better mechanisms later.

sections.title: What Counts as an Adverse Action
sections.content:
Any change to the RPKI that diminishes the set of Internet Number Resources associated with an INR holder, and that is contrary to the holder's wishes, is termed adverse. The analysis is done from the perspective of an affected INR holder. An action that results in an adverse change may be the result of an attack on a CA, an error by a CA, or an error by or an attack on a repository operator. The CA that allocated the affected resources may be acting in accordance with established policy, so the change may be contractually justified even though the holder views it as adverse. The document examines the implications of adverse actions within the RPKI with respect to resources, irrespective of the cause of the actions.

There is a second kind of harm. When a ROA or router certificate is created that competes with an existing one, the creation of the new one may itself be adverse. A newer ROA competes with an older ROA if it points to a different AS number, contains the same or a more specific prefix, and is issued by a different CA. A newer router certificate competes with an older one if it contains the same AS number, contains a different public key, and is issued by a different CA. Transferring resources or changing upstream providers may yield competing objects under some circumstances, so not all competition is an adverse action.

Adverse changes may arise from several causes. A CA may make a mistake in managing the objects it signs, or it may be subject to an attack. If an attack lets an adversary use the private key of that CA to sign objects, the effect is analogous to the CA making mistakes. There is also the possibility that a CA or repository operator may be subject to legal measures that compel them to make adverse changes. In many cases such actions are hard to distinguish from mistakes or attacks, other than in the time required to remedy them: presumably the CA will take remedial action when a mistake or an attack is detected, so the effects are similar, while a legally compelled change is likely to be slow to remedy.
sections.plainLanguage: The document asks a narrow question: if the party that signs things about your address space acts in a way you did not agree with, what breaks? The cause matters less than the effect, because a mistake, an attack and a legal order all leave the same kind of mess behind, and the only real difference is how quickly it gets cleaned up.

sections.title: The Six Actions That Can Cause Harm
sections.content:
The RPKI repository contains signed objects that are fetched and processed by relying parties. Until BGPsec is deployed, the principal goal of the RPKI is to enable a relying party to validate ROAs. A ROA binds address space to an AS number, and can be used to verify BGP announcements with respect to route origin. ROAs are the most important objects for origin validation, and all the other objects exist to enable their validation in a fashion consistent with the allocation system. Errors that result in changes to a ROA, or to objects needed to validate one, can cause relying parties to reach different conclusions about the validity of the bindings a ROA expresses. When BGPsec is deployed, router certificates will be added, and they are as important to path validation as ROAs are to origin validation.

Adverse actions take six forms.

  • Deletion (D) is removing an object from a publication point, without the permission of the INR holder.
  • Suppression (S) is not deleting an object, or not publishing an object, as intended by an INR holder. It also includes retaining a prior version of an object in a publication point when a newer version is available for publication.
  • Corruption (C) is modification of a signed object in a fashion not requiring access to the private key used to sign it, so the corrupted object will not carry a valid signature. The corrupted object implicitly replaces the legitimate version.
  • Modification (M) is publishing a syntactically valid, verifiable version of an object that differs from the existing version authorized by the INR holder. The legitimate version is implicitly deleted and replaced.
  • Revocation (R) is revoking a certificate, end entity or CA, by placing its serial number on the appropriate CRL, without authorization of the INR holder.
  • Injection (I) is introducing an instance of a signed object into a publication point without authorization of the INR holder, on the assumption that the signature will be viewed as valid by relying parties.

The first three actions can be effected by any entity that manages the publication point of the affected holder, and also by an entity able to act as a man-in-the-middle between a relying party and a repository. The latter three nominally require access to the private key of the INR holder. All six can also be effected by a parent CA, which could reissue the holder's CA certificate with a different public key matching a private key the parent holds, and then generate new signed objects with that key and publish them wherever it chooses. Most of these actions may be performed independently or in combination, for example a ROA may be revoked and deleted, or revoked and replaced with a modified ROA.
sections.plainLanguage: Six things can be done. Someone who runs the storage can remove a file, withhold a newer one, or damage it. Someone who holds the signing key can put out a different but still valid file, revoke the certificate, or add a file that was never authorised. A parent authority can do all six by issuing a replacement certificate for its child.

sections.title: What Each Action Does to Each Object
sections.content:
The document examines each object type in turn, taking the six actions in order.

CA certificates. Every INR holder is represented by one or more CA certificates, more than one when it holds resources from different sources, and more than one during key and algorithm rollover. Deleting a CA certificate stops a relying party from finding the objects the CA signed, except those it has cached, so it will not learn about new or changed bindings and cannot validate new or changed router certificates. If the missed objects were meant to replace ROAs or router certificates before they expired, valid routes may then be seen as NotFound or Invalid. Corrupting a CA certificate causes it to be rejected, which may make subordinate objects invalid. Modifying it can have several effects: changing the resource extension to exclude resources makes the objects that rely on them invalid, and changing the public key to one whose private key the parent holds lets the parent sign objects as children of that certificate, which enables modification, revocation and injection of everything underneath it.

Manifest. Each publication point contains a manifest, which enumerates by filename all the other signed objects at that point and contains a hash of each, so a relying party can tell whether the content matches what the holder intended. The manifest is what lets a relying party detect suppression or substitution of newer objects. If a manifest is modified to remove objects, those objects may be ignored; if it is modified to add objects, a valid added object will be accepted and processed; and if it lists an incorrect hash for an object, that object may be ignored. Suppressing a newer manifest makes a relying party rely on a cached one, which then does not list the new objects, so they may be ignored, with the effect of deleting them.

ROA. Deleting a ROA voids the binding between the prefix and the AS number; a relying party that previously saw it as authentic now has no evidence about it, so a legitimate route is treated as NotFound if there are no other ROAs for the prefix, or Invalid if there is another ROA with a different AS number. Suppressing a newer ROA means a change the holder intended is not effected, and relying parties may keep believing an old binding. Suppressing one of several new ROAs for the same address space makes the suppressed binding less preferred, so traffic may flow to an AS the holder did not intend. Modifying a ROA so that its AS number or address blocks differ causes the legitimate binding to be less preferred. Injecting a ROA that expresses different bindings could authorise an extra AS to originate routes for the prefix, enabling route origin spoofing, and an injected ROA expressing a longer prefix could let that AS override advertisements using shorter prefixes.

Ghostbusters Record. This is a signed object, included at the discretion of the holder or the publication point operator, that tells a relying party whom to contact when it finds a problem. Errors in it do not affect the validation of ROAs or router certificates, but deletion, suppression, corruption or revocation could stop a relying party contacting the right entity, and modification or injection could make it contact the wrong one, delaying repair.

Router certificates. These are used to verify signatures on BGPsec path attributes. Deleting one means the relying party cannot verify signatures on behalf of that AS, so the route is treated as less preferred than competing routes with valid signatures, unless another valid certificate for the same AS and public key is in use. Modifying one to represent a different AS could cause signatures to be associated with the wrong AS, so signed routes would be inconsistent with the holder's intent and traffic might be routed via a different AS than intended. Injecting one could authorise additional routers to sign BGPsec traffic for the targeted AS and undermine the BGPsec security guarantees.
sections.plainLanguage: Each object fails in its own way. Without the certificate that points to them, the objects underneath are invisible. A tampered manifest can hide a file or add one without touching either. A removed or revoked ROA makes the route look unauthorised, and a forged one can point the address space at a different network entirely. The contact record does nothing to routing but tells someone where to complain.

sections.title: Four Ways to Organise It
sections.content:
The document examines the types of problem that can arise in four scenarios, considering mistakes, successful attacks against a CA or a publication point, and situations in which a manager is compelled to act by a law enforcement authority.

Scenario A: the INR holder operates its own CA and manages its own repository publication point. Actions by the holder can adversely affect all of its resources and, transitively, resources of any subordinate CAs; if the CA is a leaf in the RPKI, the damage is limited to its own resources. Mistakes by the holder can cause any of the actions in the analysis, a successful attack against the CA can effect all of the modification, revocation or injection actions, and an attack against the publication point can effect all of the deletion, suppression or corruption actions.

Scenario B: the holder operates its own CA but outsources management of its publication point to its parent or another entity. The range of adverse effects includes those of Scenario A and adds the outsourced repository operator as a new potential source. Mistakes by the holder can cause modification, revocation or injection actions, and actions by the repository operator can affect the holder's resources and those of any subordinate CAs.

Scenario C: the holder outsources management of its CA to its parent but manages its own publication point. All signed objects are generated by the parent CA but are self-hosted. Because that CA has the private key used to sign them, it can generate alternative signed objects that the holder did not authorise; however, erroneous objects created by the parent will not be published by the holder if the holder checks them first. The document expects this scenario to be rare, because a holder that outsources CA operation seems unlikely to manage its own publication point.

Scenario D: the holder outsources both its CA and its publication point to its parent, and is the most vulnerable of the four. Actions by the parent acting on the holder's behalf can affect all signed objects associated with the holder, including subordinate CA certificates, and these will translate directly into publication point changes because the parent manages the publication point. The range of adverse effects includes those of the other three scenarios.
sections.plainLanguage: How much you can be hurt depends on who holds what. If you run both the signing key and the storage, a mistake stays with you. If someone else runs the storage, they can hide things from you. If your parent holds the key, they can sign anything on your behalf. And if your parent holds both the key and the storage, you are in the weakest position of all.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document describes a threat model for the RPKI, focusing on mistakes by or attacks against CAs and independent repository managers. It is intended to provide a basis for the design of future RPKI security mechanisms that address the concerns associated with such actions.

The analysis identifies a number of circumstances in which attacks or errors can have significant impacts on routing. The document says this should not be read as a condemnation of the RPKI, and that it is only an attempt to document the implications of a wide range of attacks and errors in the context of the RPKI. The primary alternative mechanism for disseminating routing information is Internet Routing Registry technology, which uses the Routing Policy Specification Language, and IRR technology exhibits its own set of security problems, which are discussed separately.
sections.plainLanguage: The point of the document is to make the risks concrete, not to argue against the system. The alternative to signed certificates is the older registry system, which has its own security weaknesses, so the trade-off is between two imperfect choices.

items.label: Deletion
items.desc: Removing an object from a publication point, without the permission of the INR holder.

items.label: Suppression
items.desc: Not deleting an object, or not publishing one, as the holder intended; keeping an old version when a newer one is available counts too.

items.label: Corruption
items.desc: Modifying a signed object without the private key, so the object no longer carries a valid signature.

items.label: Modification
items.desc: Publishing a syntactically valid, verifiable version of an object that differs from the one the holder authorized.

items.label: Revocation
items.desc: Revoking a certificate by putting its serial number on the appropriate CRL, without authorization.

items.label: Injection
items.desc: Introducing a signed object into a publication point without authorization, with a signature the relying party will accept.

items.title: CA certificates
items.text: Deleting one hides the objects underneath it; changing its public key lets the parent sign on the holder's behalf.

items.title: Manifest
items.text: It lists the other objects and their hashes, so an altered manifest can hide or add objects without touching them.

items.title: ROA
items.text: Deleting or revoking one voids the binding between a prefix and an AS, so the route becomes NotFound or Invalid.

items.title: Ghostbusters Record
items.text: It says who to contact about a problem; damaging it does not change validation but slows the repair.

items.title: Router certificates
items.text: Without one, signed BGPsec path attributes cannot be verified, and the route is treated as less preferred.
